title: Who is wise? (Avot 4:1)
hookLine: Ben Zoma: the wise learn from everyone; the rich are content with their lot

lines: BEN ZOMA ON THE TEMPLE MOUNT.
cards: The Talmud tells a story about a sage named Ben Zoma. One day he stood on a high step on the Temple Mount and looked down at the enormous crowds of pilgrims. Instead of being annoyed by all the people, he said a blessing.

Think how hard the first human had to work for a piece of bread, he said. Plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding, kneading, baking. And I wake up, and all of it's been done for me, by all these people.
That's the man who opens chapter four of Pirkei Avot, with four questions.

teach.b: Who is wise? Who is strong? Who is rich?
Who is honored? Each answer flips what you'd expect. Today, two of them.
Who is wise? Not the one with the most degrees.

The one who learns from every person. Then a verse from the Psalms that, in its plain sense, sounds almost boastful. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have more understanding than all my teachers."
But the Mishnah reads the Hebrew another way, which the words can bear: from all my teachers I gained understanding. Every person is a teacher. The toddler who asks why.
The coworker you find difficult. The stranger who does a job you've never noticed. Everyone knows something you don't.
Who is rich? Not the one with the most. The one who's happy with his portion, what he already has.
Another psalm backs it up: when you eat the work of your own hands, you'll be happy, and it will be well with you. Now back to the Temple Mount.
Ben Zoma looked at a huge crowd and saw bakers, farmers, weavers, all the people whose work fed and clothed him. He learned from everyone, and he was grateful for what he had.
Both begin in the same place: paying attention to the people around you, and to what you've already been given. Tomorrow, the other two questions.

how: Ben Zoma's four questions are often taught in Jewish classes, and 'who is rich? one who is happy with his portion' is a saying people quote about contentment.

games.q: you're Ben Zoma on the Temple Mount, looking down at an enormous crowd. what do you say?
o: too many people. let's go home.
a blessing, for all the people whose work feeds me.
games.why: he said a blessing, remembering the plowing, reaping and baking others did so he could eat.

practice: Think of three people you'll likely see today, including one you don't especially like, and for each one ask: what does this person know that I don't? A skill, a kind of patience, a way of seeing; there's always something.
Then, for a breath or two, notice something you already have that's enough.
